summary: Defines two parameters for the CAA DNS record: one that restricts issuance to specific accounts at a CA, identified by URIs, and another that requires particular ACME domain validation methods. These give domain owners finer control than the CA-level policy that CAA offers by default.

plainLanguage.summary: A house owner can say which locksmith may make keys, and this lets them also name the exact person and the exact way to prove who they are.

questions: what is the caa accounturi parameter
how to restrict acme issuance to one account
subtitle: Two CAA parameters that let a domain name the exact CA account, and the exact validation method, allowed to get its certificates.

tldr.problem: A CAA record can only say which Certification Authority (CA) may issue certificates for a domain. It cannot say which customer account at that CA, or which way of proving domain control, is acceptable.
tldr.mechanism: The "accounturi" parameter names the CA account allowed to request issuance, as a URI. The "validationmethods" parameter lists the validation methods the CA may use, such as ACME methods from the IANA registry.
tldr.outcome: A domain that already trusts a CA can tighten the policy further, but only if that CA documents and implements these parameters. They do nothing against CAs that ignore CAA.

today: RFC 8657 is a Proposed Standard and the data here shows no obsoleting or updating RFC. It builds on the CAA record defined in RFC 8659 and the ACME protocol in RFC 8555.

sections.title: Finer Control for CAA Records
sections.content:
The Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) DNS record, defined in RFC 8659, lets a domain publish an issuance policy for Certification Authorities (CAs). That policy has only CA-level granularity: it names a CA, not an account at the CA.

RFC 8659 also lets the "issue" and "issuewild" Properties carry CA-specific parameters. RFC 8657 defines two of them. accounturi restricts authorization to specific CA accounts identified by URIs. validationmethods limits which of a CA's domain control validation methods may be used.
sections.plainLanguage: A normal CAA record only says which company may make certificates for your website. These two extras let you also say which customer of that company and which kind of check are allowed.

sections.title: The accounturi Parameter
sections.content:
The value of accounturi MUST be a URI identifying a specific CA account. A "CA account" is an object kept by a specific CA that may request certificates and stands for an entity or group of related entities.

The parameter constrains the Property it is attached to. A CA MUST only treat that Property as authorizing issuance if it recognizes the URI as identifying the account making the request. A Property without accounturi matches any account. A Property with an invalid or unrecognized accounturi, or with more than one, is unsatisfiable.

The parameter does not replace the normal domain name check. For example, an "issue" Property naming a domain that belongs to CA A, but an account at CA B, is unsatisfiable.

For ACME, an account object MAY be identified by the URI of the ACME account object, and implementations that also implement ACME MUST recognize such URIs. CAs that do not use ACME MAY assign and recognize their own URIs.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like writing on the guest list not just the name of the hotel but the room number of the one guest who may ask for a key.

sections.title: The validationmethods Parameter
sections.content:
The value of validationmethods MUST be a comma-separated string of zero or more validation method labels. A validation method is a particular way in which a CA can validate control over a domain.

A CA MUST only treat a Property with this parameter as authorizing issuance when the method in use is one of the listed labels. Each label MUST be either a label from the IANA "ACME Validation Methods" registry or a CA-specific non-ACME label. A CA that supports both the parameter and non-ACME methods MUST assign labels to those methods. If no suitable label is in the registry, it MUST use labels beginning with ca-.

The value must match this ABNF: value = [*(label ",") label] and label = 1*(ALPHA / DIGIT / "-").
sections.plainLanguage: It is a short list of the ways someone is allowed to prove they own the website, like saying only a password or a fingerprint will do.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The parameters only help when the CA recognizes them. The CA decides what parameters mean, so domains MUST NOT assume the restrictions work unless the CA explicitly says so. CAs that implement them SHOULD document which parameters they support and whether they use DNSSEC validation for these lookups.

A CA MUST be fully consistent across all its issuance systems for a given CA domain name. A CA unable to do that MUST NOT implement support for these parameters. Account URIs must be unique across all domain names the CA recognizes as itself, and CAs SHOULD use URIs that include an authority, such as an https URI.

For DNSSEC-signed domains, the RFC says the domain SHOULD either use accounturi to allow only accounts it controls, or use only validation methods that rely solely on DNSSEC information and restrict to them with validationmethods. A CA supporting either parameter MUST do CAA validation through a trusted DNSSEC-validating resolver.

Other cautions: CAs that do not process CAA records are unaffected, CAA lookups walk up the DNS tree so delegated subdomains can escape the policy, a mistake can block legitimate requests, and because CAA records are public, account URIs are visible to third parties. CAs SHOULD also reduce the risk of stale authorizations, for example with very short validity periods or by re-checking CAA at issuance.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules only work if the locksmith agrees to follow them, and everyone can read the sign on your door, so the locksmith should not put anything secret in the names it uses.

sections.title: Example Records
sections.content:
The appendix gives zone file fragments for the domain example.com and the CA example.net. Listing two "issue" records with different accounturi values authorizes both accounts. A single record can also combine accounturi and validationmethods, so that one account may use dns-01 and another may use http-01.

Putting several methods in one comma-separated value is equivalent to publishing one record per method. A CA-specific label such as ca-foo can sit alongside registry labels like dns-01.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show what the sign on the door looks like when you name one guest, or two guests, or a guest plus the one way they must prove who they are.

viz.caption: TWO ACCOUNTS, EACH WITH ITS OWN METHOD (RFC 8657 APPENDIX A)

data.title: CAA records
data.code:
example.com. IN CAA 0 issue "example.net; \
  accounturi=https://example.net/account/1234; \
  validationmethods=dns-01"
example.com. IN CAA 0 issue "example.net; \
  accounturi=https://example.net/account/2345; \
  validationmethods=http-01"
